dhpak1.6:1.1: 1.5 The Story about Those from Kosambī Kosambakavatthu
dhpak1.6:2.2: [28.176] this Dhamma teaching was given by the Teacher while he was in residence at Jetavana with reference to the bhikkhus of Kosambī.
dhpak1.6:4.1: For at Kosambī, in Ghosita monastery, resided two bhikkhus, each with a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus.
dhpak1.6:4.2: Of the two bhikkhus, one was a bearer of the Discipline, the other a teacher of the Dhamma.
dhpak1.6:4.3: One day the teacher of the Dhamma, after easing himself, left in a vessel what remained of the water in which he had washed in the bathroom and came out.
dhpak1.6:4.4: Afterwards the bearer of the Discipline went {1.54} in and saw the water.
dhpak1.6:4.5: When he came out, he asked his companion: “Friend, was it you that left the water?”
dhpak1.6:4.6: – “Yes, friend.” – “But do you not know that it is wrong so to do?” – “Indeed I do not.”
dhpak1.6:4.7: – “But, friend, it is wrong.” – “Well then, I will make satisfaction for it.”
dhpak1.6:4.8: – “Of course, friend, if you did it unintentionally, inadvertently, it is no wrong.”
dhpak1.6:4.9: Thus the teacher of the Dhamma came to look upon the wrong as no wrong.
dhpak1.6:5.1: Notwithstanding, the bearer of the Discipline said to his own pupils: “This teacher of the Dhamma, although he has done wrong, does not realize it.”
dhpak1.6:5.2: They, seeing the pupils of the teacher of the Dhamma, said: “Your preceptor, although he has done wrong, does not realize it.”
dhpak1.6:5.3: The teacher’s pupils went and informed their own preceptor.
dhpak1.6:5.4: The teacher of the Dhamma spoke thus: “This bearer of the Discipline said before: ‘It’s no wrong,’ now he says: ‘it is wrong.’
dhpak1.6:5.5: He’s a liar.” The teacher’s pupils went and said: “Your teacher is a liar.”
dhpak1.6:5.6: Thus did they foment a quarrel between the two.
dhpak1.6:6.1: Then the bearer of the Discipline, seizing the opportunity,
dhpak1.6:6.2: pronounced sentence of suspension against the teacher of the Dhamma for failing to recognize his wrong.
dhpak1.6:6.3: Thenceforth even the supporters who furnished them with the requisites formed two factions.
dhpak1.6:6.4: Even the bhikkhunīs receiving instruction, even the protecting Devatās;
dhpak1.6:6.5: their friends and intimates, the Devatās who dwell in the sky;
dhpak1.6:6.6: beginning with these and extending to the world of Brahma, all beings, even the unattained, formed two factions.
dhpak1.6:6.7: The quarrel extended from the realm of the Four Great Kings to the heaven of the Akiniṭṭha Devas.
dhpak1.6:7.1: A Schism Now a certain bhikkhu drew near the Realised One and told him that those who pronounced
dhpak1.6:7.2: the sentence of suspension held the view that the bhikkhu had been suspended according to law;
dhpak1.6:7.3: {1.55} but that the partisans of the suspended bhikkhu held the view that he had been suspended contrary to law,
dhpak1.6:7.4: and that the latter had gathered round in support of him,
dhpak1.6:7.5: in spite of the fact that those who pronounced the sentence of suspension forbade them to do so.
dhpak1.6:8.1: Twice the Fortunate One sent word: “Let them be united,” and received [28.177] the reply: “Venerable Sir, they refuse to be united.”
dhpak1.6:8.2: The third time he exclaimed: “The assembly of bhikkhus is rent asunder!
dhpak1.6:8.3: The assembly of bhikkhus is rent asunder!”
dhpak1.6:8.4: So saying, he went to them and pointed out to those who had pronounced sentence of suspension the wrong involved in their act,
dhpak1.6:8.5: and to those who had failed to recognize the offense, the wrong involved in theirs.
dhpak1.6:8.6: Again he enjoined upon them the holding of the Uposatha and other ceremonies right there within the Boundary Hall,
dhpak1.6:8.7: and laid down the rule that those who quarreled in refectories and elsewhere were to occupy separate seats in the refectory.
dhpak1.6:9.1: Hearing that they were quarreling again, he went to them, and beginning his discourse with the words: “Enough, bhikkhus!
dhpak1.6:9.2: No quarreling!” he continued: “Bhikkhus, quarrels, strifes, contentions, disputes, all these are unprofitable.
dhpak1.6:9.3: For because of a quarrel even a tiny quail brought about the destruction of a noble elephant.”
dhpak1.6:9.4: And he told the Birth Story of the Quail.
dhpak1.6:9.5: Continuing, he said: “Bhikkhus, be united; engage not in disputes.
dhpak1.6:9.6: For because of a dispute many thousand quails lost their lives.” And he told the Birth Story of the Quail.
dhpak1.6:10.1: But in spite of this they paid no attention to his words, and a certain Dhamma teacher,
dhpak1.6:10.2: who wished the Realised One to be relieved of annoyance, said to him:
dhpak1.6:10.3: “Venerable Sir, let the Fortunate One, the lord of Dhamma, remain at home.
dhpak1.6:10.4: venerable Sir, let the Fortunate One live a life of inaction and ease in this present world.
dhpak1.6:10.5: {1.56} We shall make ourselves notorious by our quarrels, strifes, contentions, and disputes.”
dhpak1.6:11.1: Thereupon the Realised One told the following
dhpak1.6:12.1: Story of the Past: The Birth Story about King Dīghiti of Kosala
dhpak1.6:13.1: Once upon a time, bhikkhus, Brahmadatta reigned at Bārāṇasī as king of Kāsi.
dhpak1.6:13.2: Brahmadatta fought against Dīghati Kosala, took away his kingdom, and killed him while he was living in disguise.
dhpak1.6:13.3: Dīghati’s son, Prince Dīghāvu, although he knew that Brahmadatta was the murderer of his father, spared his life.
dhpak1.6:13.4: Thenceforth they were at peace with each other.
dhpak1.6:14.1: Such, bhikkhus, is said to have been the patience and gentleness of these kings who took scepter and sword.
dhpak1.6:14.2: How much more, bhikkhus, should you, who have gone forth under a Dhamma and Discipline so well taught,
dhpak1.6:14.3: let your light so shine in this world as to be known of men as patient and gentle.
dhpak1.6:14.4: Thus did the Teacher admonish them. [28.178] But in spite of his admonition he was unable to reunite them.
dhpak1.6:15.1: Thereupon, the Buddha, unhappy because of the crowded conditions under which he lived, reflected:
dhpak1.6:15.2: “Under present conditions I am crowded and jostled and live a life of discomfort.
dhpak1.6:15.3: Moreover, these bhikkhus pay no attention to what I say.
dhpak1.6:15.4: Suppose I were to retire from the haunts of men and live a life of solitude.”
dhpak1.6:16.1: After making his rounds for alms in Kosambī, without bidding the Saṅgha farewell, he took his own bowl and robe,
dhpak1.6:16.2: and went quite alone to the village of Bālaka, the salt-maker, where he discoursed to the Elder Bhagu on the solitary life;
dhpak1.6:16.3: thence he went to Eastern Bamboo Deer Park, where he discoursed to the three youths of station on the bliss of the sweets of concord;
dhpak1.6:16.4: {1.57} and from there he went to Pārileyyaka.
dhpak1.6:16.5: There, at the foot of a beautiful Sāla tree, in Protected Forest, near Pārileyyaka,
dhpak1.6:16.6: the Fortunate One spent the rainy season pleasantly, attended by the elephant Pārileyyaka.
dhpak1.6:17.1: When the lay friends resident at Kosambī went to the monastery and failed to see the Teacher, they asked:
dhpak1.6:17.2: “Venerable Sirs, where has the Teacher gone?” – “To Pārileyyaka Forest.”
dhpak1.6:17.3: – “For what reason?” – “He strove to reunite us, but we would not be reunited.”
dhpak1.6:17.4: – “Do you mean, venerable Sirs, that after receiving admission as bhikkhus at the hands of the Teacher, you refused to agree when he asked you to do so?”
dhpak1.6:17.6: “These bhikkhus, after receiving admission at the hands of the Teacher, were unwilling to patch up their differences when the Teacher asked them to do so.
dhpak1.6:17.7: It’s all their fault that we were unable to see the Teacher.
dhpak1.6:17.8: To these bhikkhus, assuredly, we will neither give seats nor offer respectful salutations or other civilities.”
dhpak1.6:17.9: And from that time on they showed them not so much as a sign of civility.
dhpak1.6:18.1: The bhikkhus got so little food that they were nearly famished,
dhpak1.6:18.2: and it required only a few days to bring them to a better state of mind.
dhpak1.6:18.3: Then they confessed their wrongs, one to another, asked to be pardoned, and said:
dhpak1.6:18.4: “Friends, we are reconciled; be to us as before.”
dhpak1.6:18.5: – “Venerable Sirs, have you begged the Teacher’s pardon?” – “No, we haven’t, friends.”
dhpak1.6:18.6: – “Well then, beg the Teacher’s pardon, and as soon as the Teacher has pardoned you, we will be to you as before.”
dhpak1.6:18.7: But as the rainy season was then at its height, they were unable to go to the Teacher and spent the rainy season very uncomfortably.
dhpak1.6:18.8: The Teacher, however, spent the time pleasantly, attended by an elephant.
dhpak1.6:18.9: For this elephant, of noble breed, left his herd {1.58} and entered the forest for the sole purpose of having a pleasant time. As it is said: [28.179]
dhpak1.6:19.1: 5b The Buddha, the Elephant, and the Monkey
dhpak1.6:20.1: “Here I live, crowded by elephants, female elephants, elephant calves, and young elephants.
dhpak1.6:20.2: They have chewed off the tips of the grass I eat; they eat branch after branch I break down; they muddy the water I have to drink.
dhpak1.6:20.3: Whenever I plunge into the water, or come up out of the water, the female elephants come and rub against my body.
dhpak1.6:20.4: Suppose I were to retire from the herd and live all alone.”
dhpak1.6:21.1: So then this noble elephant withdrew from the herd and drew near to Pārileyyaka, to Protected Forest, to the foot of the beautiful Sāla tree;
dhpak1.6:21.2: even to where the Fortunate One was, there did he draw near.
dhpak1.6:21.3: And when he had drawn near and worshipped the Fortunate One, he looked all about for a broom.
dhpak1.6:21.4: And seeing none, he smote with his foot the beautiful Sāla tree below and hewed away with his trunk at the Sāla tree above.
dhpak1.6:21.5: And taking a branch, he then swept the ground.
dhpak1.6:22.1: Then he took a waterpot in his trunk and procured drinking-water.
dhpak1.6:22.2: And as hot water was required, he prepared hot water. How was that possible?
dhpak1.6:22.3: First he produced sparks with a fire-drill which he worked with his trunk; then he dropped sticks of wood on the sparks.
dhpak1.6:22.4: Thus did he kindle a fire. In the fire he heated small stones; these he rolled along with a stick and dropped into a little depression in the rock.
dhpak1.6:22.5: Then, lowering his trunk and finding the water hot enough, he went and worshipped the Teacher.
dhpak1.6:22.6: The Teacher asked: “Is the water hot, Pārileyyaka?” and went there {1.59} and bathed.
dhpak1.6:22.7: After that the elephant brought various kinds of wild fruits and presented them to the Teacher.
dhpak1.6:23.1: Now when the Teacher entered the village for alms,
dhpak1.6:23.2: the elephant took his bowl and robe, put them on top of his head, and accompanied him.
dhpak1.6:23.3: When the Teacher reached the vicinity of the village, he bade the elephant bring him his bowl and robe, saying:
dhpak1.6:23.4: “Pārileyyaka, farther than this you are not permitted to go. Bring me my bowl and robe.”
dhpak1.6:23.5: After they were brought, the Teacher then entered the village, and the elephant stood right there until he returned.
dhpak1.6:23.6: When the Teacher returned, the elephant advanced to meet him, took his bowl and robe just as he did before,
dhpak1.6:23.7: deposited them in the Teacher’s place of abode, paid him the usual courtesies, and fanned him with the branch of a tree.
dhpak1.6:23.8: At night, to ward off danger from beasts of prey, he took a big club in his trunk, saying to himself:
dhpak1.6:23.9: “I’ll protect the Teacher,” and back and forth in the interstices of the forest he paced until sunrise.
dhpak1.6:23.10: From that time forth, [28.180] we are told, that forest was called “Protected Forest.”
dhpak1.6:24.1: When the sun rose, the elephant gave the Teacher water wherewith to bathe his face,
dhpak1.6:24.2: and in the manner before related performed all of the other duties.
dhpak1.6:25.1: Now a monkey saw the elephant up and doing each day, performing the lesser duties for the Realised One, and he said to himself: “I’ll do something too.”
dhpak1.6:25.2: One day, as he was running about, he happened to see some stick-honey free from flies.
dhpak1.6:25.3: He broke the stick off, took the honey-comb, stick and all, broke off a plantain-leaf,
dhpak1.6:25.4: placed the honey on the leaf, {1.60} and offered it to the Teacher.
dhpak1.6:25.5: The Teacher took it. The monkey watched to see whether or not he would eat it.
dhpak1.6:25.6: He observed that the Teacher, after taking the honey, sat down without eating.
dhpak1.6:25.7: “What can be the matter?” thought he.
dhpak1.6:25.8: He took hold of the stick by the tip, turned it over and over, carefully examining it as he did so, whereupon he discovered some insect’s eggs.
dhpak1.6:25.9: Having removed these gently, he again gave the honey to the Teacher. The Teacher ate it.
dhpak1.6:26.1: The monkey was so delighted that he leaped from one branch to another and danced about in great glee.
dhpak1.6:26.2: But the branches he grasped and the branches he stepped on broke off.
dhpak1.6:26.3: Down he fell on the stump of a tree and was impaled. So he died.
dhpak1.6:26.4: And solely because of his faith in the Teacher he was reborn in the Realm of the Thirty-Three in a golden mansion thirty leagues in measure,
dhpak1.6:26.5: with a retinue of a thousand Accharās, with the name Devaputta Makkaṭa.
dhpak1.6:27.1: Pure Faith It became known over all Jambudīpa that the Teacher was residing in Protected Forest, attended by a noble elephant.
dhpak1.6:27.2: From the city of Sāvatthī, Anāthapiṇḍika, Visākhā, the eminent female lay disciple,
dhpak1.6:27.3: and other such great personages sent the following message to the Elder Ānanda:
dhpak1.6:27.4: “Venerable Sir, obtain for us the privilege of seeing the Teacher.”
dhpak1.6:27.5: Likewise five hundred bhikkhus residing abroad approached the Elder Ānanda at the close of the rainy season and made the following request:
dhpak1.6:27.6: “It is a long time, Ānanda, since we have heard a discourse on the Dhamma from the lips of the Fortunate One.
dhpak1.6:27.7: We should like, brother Ānanda, if you please,
dhpak1.6:27.8: to have the privilege of hearing a discourse on the Dhamma from the lips of the Fortunate One.”
dhpak1.6:28.1: So the elder took those bhikkhus with him and went to Protected Forest.
dhpak1.6:28.2: When he reached the forest, he thought to himself: “The [28.181] Realised One has resided in solitude for a period of three months.
dhpak1.6:28.3: It is therefore not fitting that I should approach him all at once with so many bhikkhus as these.”
dhpak1.6:28.4: {1.61} Accordingly he left those bhikkhus outside and approached the Teacher quite alone.
dhpak1.6:29.1: When the elephant Pārileyyaka saw the elder, he took his staff and rushed forward.
dhpak1.6:29.2: The Teacher looked around and said to the elephant: “Come back, Pārileyyaka;
dhpak1.6:29.3: do not drive him away. He is an attendant of the Buddha.”
dhpak1.6:29.4: The elephant immediately threw away his staff and requested the privilege of taking the elder’s bowl and robe.
dhpak1.6:29.5: The elder refused. The elephant thought to himself:
dhpak1.6:29.6: “If he is versed in the rules of etiquette, he will refrain from placing his monastic requisites on the stone slab where the Teacher is accustomed to sit.”
dhpak1.6:29.7: The elder placed his bowl and robe on the ground.
dhpak1.6:29.8: For those who are versed in the rules of etiquette never place their own monastic requisites on the seat or bed of their spiritual superiors.
dhpak1.6:30.1: The elder, after saluting the Teacher, seated himself on one side.
dhpak1.6:30.2: The Teacher asked him: “Did you come alone?”
dhpak1.6:30.3: The elder informed him that he had come with five hundred bhikkhus. “But where are they?” asked the Teacher.
dhpak1.6:30.4: “I did not know how you would feel about it, and therefore I left them outside and came in alone.”
dhpak1.6:30.5: – “Tell them to come in.” The elder did so. The Teacher exchanged friendly greetings with the bhikkhus.
dhpak1.6:31.1: Then the bhikkhus said to the Teacher: “Venerable Sir, the Fortunate One is a refined Buddha, a refined prince.
dhpak1.6:31.2: You must have endured much hardship, standing and sitting here alone as you have during these three months.
dhpak1.6:31.3: For of course you had no one to perform the major and minor duties for you,
dhpak1.6:31.4: no one to offer you water for bathing the face or to perform any of the other duties for you.”
dhpak1.6:32.1: The Teacher replied: “Bhikkhus, the elephant Pārileyyaka performed all of these offices for me.
dhpak1.6:32.2: For one who obtains such a companion as he may well live alone;
dhpak1.6:32.3: did one fail to find such, {1.62} even so the life of solitude were better for him.”
dhpak1.6:32.4: So saying, he pronounced these three verses in the Chapter about the Elephant:
dhpak1.6:33.1: Dhp 328. If you find a prudent, wise friend or companion who lives well,
dhpak1.6:33.2: overcoming all your troubles live with that one, glad and mindful.
dhpak1.6:34.1: Dhp 329. If you find a prudent, wise friend or companion who lives well,
dhpak1.6:34.2: like a king who abandons his conquered kingdom live alone like an elephant in the forest. [28.182]
dhpak1.6:35.1: Dhp 330. It is better to live alone, there is no friendship with a fool,
dhpak1.6:35.2: one should live alone and not do wicked things, unconcerned, like an elephant in the forest.
dhpak1.6:36.1: At the conclusion of the verses the five hundred bhikkhus were established in Arahatship.
dhpak1.6:37.1: The Elder Ānanda then delivered the message sent by Anāthapiṇḍika and the rest, saying:
dhpak1.6:37.2: “Venerable Sir, 50 million noble disciples headed by Anāthapiṇḍika desire your return.”
dhpak1.6:37.3: – “Very well,” said the Teacher, “take bowl and robe.” Causing them to take bowl and robe, he set out.
dhpak1.6:37.4: The elephant went and stood crosswise on the road. “Venerable Sir, what is the elephant doing?”
dhpak1.6:37.5: – “Bhikkhus, he desires to give alms to you. For a long time he has served me; it is not right to hurt his feelings.
dhpak1.6:37.6: Turn back, bhikkhus!” The Teacher and the bhikkhus {1.63} turned back.
dhpak1.6:37.7: The elephant entered the forest, gathered bananas and various other fruits, heaped them together, and on the following day gave them to the bhikkhus.
dhpak1.6:37.8: The five hundred bhikkhus were unable to dispose of them all.
dhpak1.6:37.9: When they had finished eating, the Teacher took bowl and robe and set out.
dhpak1.6:37.10: The elephant, threading his way through the bhikkhus, went and stood crosswise in front of the Teacher.
dhpak1.6:38.1: “Venerable Sir, what is the elephant doing?”
dhpak1.6:38.2: – “Bhikkhus, having spied your parting, he desires to make me turn back.”
dhpak1.6:38.3: Said the Teacher to the elephant: “Pārileyyaka, I am going now, never to return.
dhpak1.6:38.4: You cannot hope in this existence to enter into states of absorption, or to attain spiritual insight, or the paths, or the fruitions.
dhpak1.6:38.5: Halt!” When the elephant heard that, he thrust his trunk into his mouth and retreated very slowly, weeping as he went.
dhpak1.6:38.6: Could he have made the Teacher turn back, he would have cared for him in the very same way to the end of his days.
dhpak1.6:39.1: Now when the Teacher reached the vicinity of the village, he said: “Pārileyyaka, farther than this it is unsafe for you to go.
dhpak1.6:39.2: The habitations of men are fraught with danger to you. Halt!” The elephant halted where he was and wept.
dhpak1.6:39.3: As the Teacher slowly passed out of sight, he died of a broken heart.
dhpak1.6:39.4: Through faith in the Teacher he was reborn in the Realm of the Thirty-Three in a golden mansion thirty leagues in measure,
dhpak1.6:39.5: with a retinue of a thousand Accharās. Devaputta Pārileyyaka was his name.
dhpak1.6:40.1: The Teacher arrived in due course at Jetavana.
dhpak1.6:40.2: The bhikkhus of Kosambī, {1.64} hearing of the Teacher’s return to Sāvatthī, went there to beg his pardon.
dhpak1.6:40.3: The king of Kosala, hearing [28.183] that the quarrelsome bhikkhus of Kosambī had come to Sāvatthī, approached the Teacher and said:
dhpak1.6:40.4: “Venerable Sir, I’ll not allow those bhikkhus to come into my country.”
dhpak1.6:40.5: – “Great king, these bhikkhus are good men; only because of a dispute they had with each other they paid no attention to my words.
dhpak1.6:40.6: Now they are coming to beg my pardon; let them come, great king.”
dhpak1.6:41.1: Anāthapiṇḍika also said: “I’ll not allow those bhikkhus to enter the monastery.”
dhpak1.6:41.2: But the Teacher took issue with him as he had with the king, and he was silent.
dhpak1.6:42.1: Now when those bhikkhus reached Sāvatthī, the Fortunate One gave orders that separate lodging should be prepared and given to them.
dhpak1.6:42.2: The other bhikkhus neither sit nor stand in their company.
dhpak1.6:42.3: One after another those who came asked the Teacher: “Where, venerable Sir, are the quarrelsome bhikkhus of Kosambī?”
dhpak1.6:42.4: The Teacher pointed them out, saying: “There they are!”
dhpak1.6:42.6: One after another those who came pointed their fingers at them, until for shame they were unable to lift their heads.
dhpak1.6:42.7: Then they threw themselves at the feet of the Fortunate One and asked him to pardon them.
dhpak1.6:43.1: The Teacher said: “Bhikkhus, grievous was the wrong you committed when,
dhpak1.6:43.2: after receiving admission as bhikkhus at the hands of a Buddha like me,
dhpak1.6:43.3: in spite of my efforts to reconcile you, you refused to obey my words.
dhpak1.6:43.4: Even wise men of old hearkened to the admonition of their mother and father under sentence of death, {1.65} disobeyed it not,
dhpak1.6:43.5: even while their parents were being deprived of life, and afterwards established their sovereignty over two kingdoms.”
dhpak1.6:44.1: So saying, he related the Kosambika Birth Story once more, concluding as follows:
dhpak1.6:44.2: “Thus, bhikkhus, Prince Dīghāvu, even while his mother and father were being deprived of life, disobeyed not their admonition and afterwards,
dhpak1.6:44.3: obtaining Brahmadatta’s daughter in marriage, bore sway over the two kingdoms of Kāsi and Kosala.
dhpak1.6:44.4: You, however, disobeyed my words, and thereby committed a grievous wrong.”
dhpak1.6:44.5: So saying, he pronounced the following verse:
dhpak1.6:45.1: 6. Pare ca na vijānanti mayam-ettha yamāmase,
dhpak1.6:45.2: ye ca tattha vijānanti tato sammanti medhagā.
dhpak1.6:46.1: The others do not understand that we should restrain ourselves here,
dhpak1.6:46.2: but for those who do understand, through that, their dissensions do cease. {1.66}
dhpak1.6:47.1: At the conclusion of the verse the assembled bhikkhus
dhpak1.6:47.2: were established in the fruition of Stream-entry.
